Title: Rethinking Layer Redundancy in Large Language Models: Calibration Objectives and Search for Depth Pruning
Text:
Rethinking Layer Redundancy in Large Language
Models: Calibration Objectives and Search for Depth
Pruning
Minkyu Kim1,†, Vincent-Daniel Yun1, 2,†∗, Youngrae Kim2†, YoungJin Heo1,
Suin Cho1,3, Seong-hun Kim1, Woosang Lim1,4, Gaeul Kwon1,2
1Neural Superintelligence Lab, MODULABS, Republic of Korea
2University of Southern California, United States
3Boston University, United States
4Seoul National University, Republic of Korea
Abstract
Depth pruning improves the inference efficiency of large language models by
removing Transformer blocks. Prior work has focused on importance criteria
and search algorithms, often treating layer redundancy as an inherent structural
property of pretrained networks. In contrast, we adopt a functional perspective,
where redundancy is jointly influenced by the model and the evaluation objective,
suggesting that a universal ranking may not be sufficient. Through an empirical
study across three LLM families, two calibration objectives, and seven search algo-
rithms, we observe that different objectives yield qualitatively different redundant
layers, and that perplexity and downstream accuracy rankings do not consistently
align. Under a fixed objective, however, search algorithms tend to produce similar
solutions. Overall, our results suggest that the calibration objective may play a
more influential role than the choice of search algorithm, indicating that further
attention to objective design could be beneficial.
1
Introduction
Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved strong capabilities, but their scale incurs substantial
deployment cost [5, 21]. Among structured compression approaches, depth pruning removes entire
Transformer blocks, reducing inference cost proportionally to the number of pruned layers [10, 17].
Prior work advances depth pruning along two axes, importance criteria [10, 17, 20, 24] and search
algorithms [2, 9, 16, 17, 19]. Several of these works treat layer importance as an intrinsic property of
the pretrained network: ShortGPT [10] ranks layers by cosine similarity independent of downstream
tasks, and related similarity- and magnitude-based criteria [2, 17] apply a single ranking across uses.
We refer to this as the structural view, where layer redundancy is assumed to be a property of the
pretrained model, recoverable by an appropriate criterion or search.
We examine whether this structural view is consistent with the empirical behavior of LLMs under
pruning. Our central observation is that layer redundancy may be better understood as a functional
property jointly influenced by the model and the evaluation objective: a layer identified as redundant
under language modeling perplexity may remain important for downstream reasoning. This suggests
that the appropriate object of study is not a single universal ranking, but an objective-conditioned
notion of redundancy.

To provide empirical evidence, we disentangle the two design axes. Prior work typically varies the
importance metric and search algorithm jointly, making it difficult to attribute observed gains to either
component [9, 24]. We instead hold one axis fixed while varying the other, casting depth pruning as
the subset selection problem

and comparing seven search algorithms under two distinct calibration objectives on three LLM
families: language modeling perplexity on C4, and a task likelihood margin [20] on commonsense
reasoning [6].
Three empirical findings support this perspective. First, the same model exhibits different pruning
patterns under different objectives: under perplexity, removals concentrate in contiguous mid-to-late
layers and are largely consistent across search algorithms, whereas under the task likelihood margin,
removals are more distributed and vary across algorithms. Second, for perplexity-pruned models,
perplexity rank and downstream accuracy rank do not consistently align: Spearman correlations range
from ρ = −0.78 to near zero, with most conditions negative. Third, within a fixed objective, search
algorithms converge to similar solutions, with average accuracy differences of 1–3 percentage points.
These results indicate that the calibration objective may play a more influential role than the choice
of search algorithm.
Contributions. We articulate and empirically examine a functional view of layer redundancy in
LLM depth pruning. We disentangle search and objective across three LLM families, two calibration
objectives, and seven search algorithms in a controlled setting. Finally, we identify a systematic
misalignment between calibration perplexity and downstream reasoning accuracy as an empirical
consequence of objective-dependent redundancy.
2
Related Works
Pruning paradigms. Unstructured pruning [4, 18, 22] can achieve high sparsity, but often relies
on specialized hardware to realize practical speedups. In contrast, structured pruning removes
architectural components, enabling immediate efficiency gains on standard hardware. Among
structured approaches, depth pruning removes entire Transformer blocks deemed redundant [17],
with inference cost scaling approximately linearly with the number of retained layers.
Importance criteria. A substantial line of work focuses on designing importance criteria to identify
redundant layers, including cosine similarity [10], inter-layer output similarity [17], mutual infor-
mation [24], and prompt-conditioned routing [20]. These approaches share a common premise: that
each layer admits an intrinsic notion of importance that can be recovered by an appropriate criterion.
Under this view, once a reliable ranking is obtained, it can be applied across tasks and settings. We
revisit this assumption and examine whether redundancy is better understood as a property of the
layer itself or as dependent on the evaluation objective.
Search strategies and the metric-search confound. Most pruning frameworks combine an im-
portance metric with a search procedure. One-shot [10] and greedy iterative [17] methods make
sequential and often irreversible decisions, which has motivated the use of more global approaches
such as evolutionary search [16] and constrained binary optimization [9] for the underlying NP-hard
subset selection problem [12]. However, these global methods typically introduce both a new metric
and a new search strategy simultaneously, making it difficult to isolate the source of observed im-
provements. In this work, we explicitly disentangle these two axes by holding one component fixed
while varying the other. The prior-guided GA and BO variants we employ are used as controlled
search procedures rather than as standalone contributions.
3
Depth Pruning as Subset Selection
3.1
Notation and problem formulation
Let fθ0 denote a pretrained LLM with N transformer blocks, indexed by I ≜{1, . . . , N}. We
assume access to a small calibration dataset D and an evaluation loss L(D; θ); throughout this work,
L is instantiated as either the negative log-likelihood or a task likelihood margin loss [20]. A pruning
decision is represented by a subset S ⊆I of removed layers, with induced mask (mS)i ≜⊮[i /∈S];

3.2
Non-additivity of layer removal
A central challenge in solving equation (2) is that the effect of removing multiple layers is non-additive.
Define ∆(S) ≜L(D; θ0 ⊙mS) −L(D; θ0). For disjoint subsets S1, S2 ⊆I, in general
∆(S1 ∪S2) ̸= ∆(S1) + ∆(S2),
(3)
because removing layer i alters the hidden-state distribution seen by all subsequent layers, a phe-
nomenon known as reconstruction error explosion [8]. A methodological consequence is that layer
selection is not an independent ranking problem: a per-layer score si that approximates ∆({i})
cannot, in general, predict the joint effect ∆(S) for |S| > 1. Top-k ranking over such scores therefore
implicitly assumes an additivity that the architecture does not provide.
3.3
Redundancy as a property of (θ0, L, D)
Equation (2) further makes explicit that the optimal subset S⋆is a property of the triple (θ0, L, D),
not of θ0 alone. Fixing θ0 and varying L can, in principle, yield entirely different minimizers, since
two losses may assign different importance to the same hidden-state distortions. We therefore adopt
a relational definition: a layer i ∈I is functionally redundant with respect to L if i ∈S⋆for some
optimal or near-optimal subset of equation (2). Under this definition, the structural view implicit
in prior work corresponds to the assumption that the functionally redundant set is approximately
invariant to L, so that a single universal ranking suffices. The functional view investigated here is
its negation. Equation (2) allows us to test between the two by fixing θ0, D and separately varying
the search procedure and the loss L: small variation under the former combined with large variation
under the latter constitutes direct evidence for the functional view, and this decomposition organizes
Section 5.
4
Experimental Setup
For each pruned model, we independently vary the search algorithm while fixing the calibration
objective, and vice versa, isolating the two sources of variation in S⋆. All datasets used are publicly
available NLP benchmarks; no human-subject data was collected. We evaluate three open-weight
LLMs of comparable scale but differing training pipelines: LLaMA3 8B, LLaMA3.1 8B, and Qwen3
8B, to check whether observed phenomena are specific to a single pretraining recipe or recur across
model families.
Reproducibility.
All experiments were conducted on 4 NVIDIA A40 GPUs.
Calibration objectives.
We consider two qualitatively different losses L in equation (2): language
modeling perplexity on C4 [14] (64 samples, 2048 tokens each), and a task likelihood margin
loss [20] (the average log-likelihood gap between correct and incorrect answers; 128 samples from
Commonsense 170k [7]). The two represent distinct styles of supervision: perplexity is a task-
agnostic fluency signal, whereas the task margin is a discriminative, task-centric signal. If redundancy
were structural, both should reward similar subsets.
Search algorithms.
Under each objective, we compare seven algorithms spanning the locality
spectrum: one-shot top-k selection, greedy iterative deletion [17], beam search (B = 5), prior-guided
genetic algorithm (GA; population 16, elitism 0.2, mutation 0.15, 10 generations), prior-guided
Bayesian optimization (BO; 200 trials, 10 random inits), constrained binary optimization (CBO) [9],
and fast-block-select [24]. These serve as a controlled panel of search behaviors rather than competing
method proposals; all share the same L and D within each cell.

Pruning budgets.
We examine two budgets k ∈7, 9, spanning moderate to high compression
of the roughly 32–40 blocks in each model, from regimes where one-shot is typically considered
adequate (k = 7) to regimes where reconstruction error becomes more pronounced (k = 9).
Evaluation.
Evaluation is aligned with the calibration objective to avoid confounding calibration
loss with evaluation metric. Perplexity-pruned models are evaluated on WikiText-2 [11], C4 [14],
and LAMBADA [13]. Task-likelihood-pruned models are evaluated zero-shot on HellaSwag [23],
WinoGrande [15], ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge [3], PIQA [1], and BoolQ.
5
Evidence for a Functional View of Redundancy
We present three empirical findings supporting the functional view of Section 3: (i) the calibration
objective qualitatively reshapes which layers are selected as redundant (§5.1); (ii) perplexity rank
and downstream accuracy rank are not positively correlated (§5.2); and (iii) within a single objective,
different search algorithms converge to similar solutions (§5.3).

5.1
Objectives reshape patterns
Figure 1 visualizes which layers are removed by each search algorithm under each calibration
objective. Under the structural view, the two halves should look broadly similar: if a layer is
intrinsically redundant in θ0, both objectives should select it.
The observed patterns are inconsistent with this prediction. Under perplexity calibration, pruning
concentrates in two contiguous architectural clusters (indices 9–12 and 22–26 in LLaMA3 8B; similar
mid-and-late clusters appear in LLaMA3.1 8B and Qwen3 8B), and this clustering is largely shared
across search algorithms. Under the task likelihood margin on the same model, removals are scattered
across the network and vary more strongly between search algorithms. The two objectives therefore
produce structurally different redundant sets, not merely different rankings of the same structure: the

5.2
Perplexity vs. accuracy
Do the two objectives at least agree on which pruning decisions preserve model quality at the outcome
level? For each (model, M) combination, we rank the seven perplexity-pruned models by average
calibration perplexity and by average downstream accuracy, and compare the two rankings.

Under the structural view, both rankings should agree. The observed Spearman correlations (Figure 2)
instead range from ρ = −0.78 to values near zero, with no condition showing a strong positive
correlation and five of six being negative. The pruned model that best preserves perplexity is therefore
not the one that best preserves reasoning. Under the functional view, this is expected: perplexity and
task margin define distinct redundancy landscapes, and subsets optimal for one are not, in general,
optimal for the other.

If objectives define different redundancy landscapes, it remains to ask how much of the variation we
attribute to the objective actually reflects search noise. Figure 3 quantifies the within-objective spread
across the seven search algorithms. For task-likelihood-pruned models (Figure 3a), inter-method
accuracy variance is small across conditions (σ2 = 0.7–5.7), with Qwen3 at M = 9 as the only
outlier (σ2 = 11.0). Consequently, switching the search algorithm under a fixed objective moves
average accuracy by only 1–3 percentage points (Table 1): on LLaMA3 8B at M = 7, the seven
algorithms span the range 57.63–60.90%.
For perplexity-pruned models (Figure 3b), within-objective variance is similarly tight at M = 7
on LLaMA3 and LLaMA3.1 (σ2 = 1.1, 0.2) but grows at M = 9 and on Qwen3 as some search
procedures (notably CBO and fast-block-select) produce reconstruction error explosion. Even so,
the high-variance cases reflect a small number of outlier failures rather than a smooth spread: most
algorithms still cluster in a narrow band. We note that search choice does matter in the regime
where some procedures fail catastrophically (CBO and fast-block-select on Qwen3); our claim is
that conditional on reasonable search, objective dominates. Changing the objective while holding
the search fixed, by contrast, reconfigures S⋆at the layer level (Figure 1), flips the sign of the
perplexity–accuracy correlation (§5.2), and on Qwen3 8B at M = 7 reverses which objective yields
higher accuracy. Within-objective variation perturbs an outcome; cross-objective variation changes
which landscape is being optimized.
The cost-benefit profile of search.
This has a direct practical reading (Table 3): on LLaMA3 8B at
M = 7 under task-likelihood pruning, one-shot and fast-block-select finish in under 10 minutes (550s
and 429s) at 57.99% average accuracy; prior-guided BO takes roughly 70 minutes (4,233s) to reach
60.90%; beam search takes nearly 4 hours (13,869s) for 60.12%. The gap between the cheapest and
the most accurate is under 3 percentage points, well within the within-objective band. Under the
functional view, this is expected: once L is chosen, the landscape admits near-optimal subsets under
even simple search, and sophisticated search yields diminishing returns. The lever with outsized
effect is the choice of L, which is essentially free.

Taken together, Sections 5.1–5.3 show that varying search under a fixed objective produces small,
bounded movement, whereas varying the objective under a fixed search produces qualitatively
different subsets, uncorrelated rankings, and occasional reversals. In LLM depth pruning, the
objective, rather than the network or the search, is the primary determinant of redundancy.
6
Conclusion
We examine whether layer redundancy in LLM depth pruning is structural or jointly determined
by the evaluation objective. By disentangling search and objective across models, objectives, and
algorithms, we find evidence consistent with the functional view: objectives induce different pruning
patterns, perplexity and accuracy rankings do not align, and search algorithms yield similar solutions
under a fixed objective. These results suggest that the calibration objective may be more influential
than the choice of search algorithm, and that more complex search provides limited additional benefit
once the objective is fixed.

Abstract: Depth pruning improves the inference efficiency of large language models by removing Transformer blocks. Prior work has focused on importance criteria and search algorithms, often treating layer redundancy as an inherent structural property of pretrained networks. In contrast, we adopt a functional perspective, where redundancy is jointly influenced by the model and the evaluation objective, suggesting that a universal ranking may not be sufficient. Through an empirical study across three LLM families, two calibration objectives, and seven search algo- rithms, we observe that different objectives yield qualitatively different redundant layers, and that perplexity and downstream accuracy rankings do not consistently align. Under a fixed objective, however, search algorithms tend to produce similar solutions. Overall, our results suggest that the calibration objective may play a more influential role than the choice of search algorithm, indicating that further attention to objective design could be beneficial.
